title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a model hallucination failure occurring at the point of professional output, specifically legal citation work. An AI tool used to help draft court motions fabricated case citations, case titles, and quoted language that did not exist. The failure reached filed court documents across multiple submissions before opposing counsel or the court identified it. The attorney who used the tool believed it performed accuracy checks, which it did not, meaning no independent verification step was built into her workflow and none was applied before filing.

The failure mode is straightforward: a language model asserting nonexistent legal authority as fact, in a context where factual precision is a core professional and legal obligation. It was not caught before filing because the supervising attorney was unaware AI had been used and no separate citation-verification process was applied to the AI output. Manual cross-checking of each cited case against a legal database before filing would have been sufficient to catch it.

It is not established that the use of fabricated citations affected any ruling, that the plaintiff's claims about her losses have been adjudicated, or that any party acted with intent to deceive. The case was pending trial as of the reporting date.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after being caught using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving a Los Angeles homeowner. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by storm damage and delayed repairs. She claims the delays and incomplete work led her family to drain their savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. State Farm argued she failed to file within a year and blamed negligence by the plaintiff and contractors.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, believing it performed accuracy checks when it did not. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Her supervising attorney, Kenneth Katel, took responsibility despite not knowing AI was used. The case goes to trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI, and a database tracking 1,922 documented cases of legal AI hallucinations worldwide.
